newsitem.title: ITALY: Some EU countries want Italy out of EMU - minister.
newsitem.headline: Some EU countries want Italy out of EMU - minister.

text.p: Italian Finance Minister Vincenzo Visco said on Monday that some of Italy's European partners wanted to keep the country out of a single currency.

He made his allegation following criticism from opposition politicians and business leaders of a stringent 1997 budget unveiled last Friday to help Italy meet the criteria for membership of the planned currency union in 1999.

The package aims to cut 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) from next year's deficit, almost double the centre-left government's initial target, and includes a special one-off "Euro-tax" to raise 13 trillion lire.
Visco told a news conference called to discuss fiscal aspects of the budget that the government had changed its approach to drafting the budget earlier this month.

"The government line changed because there was an acceleration towards convergence in some countries linked not only to the conviction but also to the hope and desire that our country would be excluded," Visco said.
He would not name the countries.
"Obviously there are no official statements about this but the situation has changed at an international level with respect to the summer," Visco said.
Italy, a founder member of the original European Economic Community (EEC), has historically been acutely sensitive to any suggestion that it is not the equal of its European partners.
Any hint of foreign criticism is often taken as an affront to the nation and can serve to unite Italians.

The 1997 budget package, which now goes to parliament, aims to ensure Italy approaches the three percent ratio of deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) required under the Maastricht treaty for joining economic and monetary union from the start.
The government had to revise its package dramatically after a meeting between Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi and Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar earlier this month.
Italy had been looking to Spain to support its tentative bid to persuade European partners to relax stringent criteria for countries wishing to be part of EMU but Aznar refused.

"He wanted Spain and Italy to walk together holding hands towards Maastricht...I am not interested in holding hands. I told him we'd be there right at the start," the Financial Times newspaper on Monday quoted Aznar as saying.
